I'm Matheus, a full-stack engineer who takes ideas from zero to pitch fast.

Looking for: geospatial/Python (GDAL, rasterio), planetary science or geology, a UI/UX designer who likes maps, and a storyteller for the pitch.
summary: Armstrong Maps is a mission-planning tool a crew would use aboard the spacecraft before an astronaut goes down to the surface of Mars. On the ship's console, the crew picks a landing site on a 3D globe, stacks real NASA data over it and draws the route of the walk. The plan is checked before anyone steps outside and returns a go, caution or no-go verdict with its reasons: life support, the distance to walk back, the radiation dose measured by Curiosity, space weather forecast by NASA's DONKI, daylight from NASA/JPL Horizons, and ground too steep to walk from NASA elevation models. It also shows how the astronaut's helmet visor would carry that same plan on the surface: heading, next waypoint, life support left, time to turn back, dose and a map of the route, over real rover panoramas, in step with the ship. Everything is built on NASA open data, and every number carries its source or a label saying it is simulated or assumed. Its purpose is simple: the success and the safety of every walk on Mars.
details:
Summary

Armstrong Maps is a layered map of Mars that integrates data from multiple NASA sources into an all-in-one platform designed to guide astronauts during their missions.

The platform is built as a web application that astronauts can use aboard their spacecraft to plan exploration routes and visualize data. It is also accessible on mobile devices that astronauts can carry during surface exploration. Finally, the Astronaut Visor view simulates a helmet display, showing essential information while an astronaut carries out a mission. (More information in Astronaut Visor section).

Expected Impact

Armstrong Maps aims to make Mars exploration safer and more accessible by bringing NASA data available for selected exploration sites into a single, interactive platform. Its spacecraft view helps crew members visualize terrain, plan routes, and assess potential hazards, while its Astronaut Visor view provides essential mission information during surface exploration. Communication features connect the astronaut in the field with the spacecraft crew, allowing them to exchange messages and flags to coordinate activities. By combining these tools with Go, No-Go, and Caution risk assessments, the project demonstrates how scientific data can support informed decisions before and during a mission.

Full documentation of the project: https://www.armstrongmaps.us/docs
Github Repository: https://github.com/matheusdenigris/armstrong-maps

Features

The features available in the project can be described in the following sections: Mars Globe, Visiting a Site and Astronaut Visor.

Mars Globe

The landing page features an interactive Mars globe highlighting exploration sites. These locations were selected based on previous exploration sites and the availability of data in NASA Mars Trek.


Visiting a Site

Selecting a site opens a detailed map of the area. From this view, users can explore data and access mission tools through panels on the left and right sides of the screen. Where data is available, the map also displays the routes traveled by the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers and the location of the InSight lander. The base location considered in this project is the same as other missions for each location.

In the left panel, users can toggle map layers to display topography, terrain relief, and other information, providing an overview of the exploration site. The available layers and their data sources are described in the Map Layers section.

The right panel contains four tabs: Walk, Link, Site, and Photos.


Walk

The Walk tab allows users to plan an exploration route by selecting points on the map. It displays the distance from the base, the total distance along the selected route, and a Go, No-Go, or Caution recommendation for the planned walk.

This tab also provides access to the Astronaut Visor view, which simulates the information an astronaut would see during a mission.

Route planning and the criteria behind these recommendations are explained in the Plan a Walk section. The visor interface is described in the Astronaut Visor section.

Link

The Link tab displays mission progress and allows crew members aboard the spacecraft to send messages and flags to the astronaut exploring the surface. These updates appear in the astronaut’s helmet display.


Site

The Site tab displays key information about the selected location, including the Mars clock, weather conditions, radiation, and Curiosity’s route, where applicable. It also shows air temperature and atmospheric pressure over the past 30 days, along with wind information. The data sources for each element are described in the Site section.


Photos

The Photos tab retrieves mission images related to the selected site from the NASA Image and Video Library.

Astronaut Visor

The Astronaut Visor simulates a 360° view from inside an astronaut’s helmet while following the planned exploration route. It uses images of the selected site from the NASA Image and Video Library to create a visual representation of the surroundings. If 360° images from the site are not available, the app uses a vision from another location, to simulate the environment. This information can be retrieved in the “Sources” button, available on the Visor page.

The interface also displays life-support information, mission progress (such as the number of waypoints visited) and environmental data, including radiation, air temperature, and atmospheric pressure, when available.

Data Source and Assumptions

Map Layers
The map layers that are available in the application are:

  1. Steep ground
    1. Slopes computed from NASA elevation models, to show ground too steep to walk.
    2. Source: Mars Global Digital Dune Database
    1. Identifies mapped areas of loose-sand dunes within the selected exploration site, helping users recognize terrain that may be difficult to traverse and account for it when planning routes. Where available, slip-face directions provide additional information about dune orientation.
    2. Source: Mars Global Digital Dune Database
    1. Combines colour-coded elevation with shaded terrain to highlight hills, valleys, craters, and other landforms. This layer helps users understand the surrounding landscape and consider elevation changes when planning exploration routes.
    2. Source: MGS MOLA and Mars Express HRSC, Color Hillshade Blend
    1. Highlights terrain features through differences in surface heating, with warmer, sun-facing slopes appearing brighter than cooler, shaded slopes.
    2. Source: MO THEMIS-IR Day, Global Mosaic
    1. Highlights differences in how surface materials retain heat after sunset, helping users distinguish rocky areas from surfaces covered in fine dust or sand.
    2. Source: MO THEMIS-IR Night, Global Mosaic
    1. Shows how well surface materials store and release heat, helping users distinguish areas of rock or compacted ground from loose dust and sand.
    2. Source: MGS TES, Global Thermal Inertia
    1. Identifies areas where accumulated dust may obscure the underlying terrain and limit the interpretation of surface composition. It helps users locate relatively dust-free areas for geological investigation.
    2. Source: MGS TES, Global Dust
    1. Highlights estimated concentrations of sheet silicates and silica-rich glass, helping users identify potential targets for geological investigation. These materials are mapped as a combined group, so the layer provides regional context rather than confirming individual clay deposits.
    2. Source: MGS TES, Global Sheet Silicates/High-Si Glass

Plan a Walk

Users can plan a walk by selecting waypoints on the map and setting the task and work time at each stop. The route starts at the base, passes through the selected points, and includes a straight return to the base. The Walk panel displays the total distance, estimated time outside, life support used, and radiation dose.

Each plan receives a go, caution, or no-go recommendation based on the following criteria:

  1. Life support: The spacesuit provides 8 hours of life support. A walk exceeding this duration receives a no-go.
  2. Radiation: The project's daily radiation limit is set at 0.64 mSv per astronaut. A walk exceeding this dose receives a no-go.
  3. Space weather: Data from NASA’s DONKI service is checked for coronal mass ejections (CMEs) forecast to reach Mars during the walk. A CME around the walk adds a caution.
  4. Return distance: Astronauts must remain within 5 km of the base to stay within the walk-back limit.
  5. Terrain slope: A slope of 15° or more raises a caution, while a slope of 25° or more results in a no-go.
  6. Daylight: A Sun elevation below 10° raises a caution, while a walk in darkness receives a no-go.
  7. Dune fields: A route crossing a mapped dune field receives a no-go.

The estimated time outside assumes a walking speed of 2.5 km/h and includes the work time set for each stop. A plan can be shared as a link and opens on another device. During the walk, the base calculates whether it still has line of sight to the astronaut. This is calculated by modeling the ground between them using NASA elevation data, then draws an imaginary straight line from the 5 m antenna mast at the base to an antenna mounted on the astronaut’s helmet, about 2 m above the ground. If terrain or Mars’s curved surface crosses that line, the radio link is lost.
Every distance uses the radius of Mars (3,389.5 km).

Site

The site tab contains the data below:

  1. Mars Clock
    1. Shows the current local solar time, Sun elevation, sunset or sunrise, daylight remaining, mean solar time, Mars Sol Date, season, and the next sunrise or sunset.
    2. Source: NASA/JPL Horizons, Mars24 Algorithm
    1. Shows the latest Curiosity REMS weather at Gale Crater: air and ground temperature, pressure, sky description, ultraviolet, sunrise, and sunset. Away from Gale, it is shown as a reference. At Jezero, it also shows Perseverance MEDA’s last available air temperature, pressure, sunrise, sunset, and season measurement. This is based on historical data, as we don't have the current weather.
    2. Source: Curiosity REMS and Perseverance MEDA.
    1. Shows the published surface-radiation average: 0.64 ± 0.12 mSv per Earth day. It is an average measured by Curiosity at Gale Crater, not a live reading.
    2. Source: MSL RAD, Hassler et al. (2014).
    1. Shows NASA DONKI forecasts of coronal mass ejections reaching Mars, including significant, minor, and glancing arrivals. It also shows solar energetic particle events from the last 30 days. CME arrivals are model forecasts, not measurements on Mars. Particle events are detected near Earth.
    2. Source: NASA DONKI
    1. At Gale, shows Curiosity’s latest sol, distance driven, and latest position. The white map line is its traverse since landing. Jezero shows the equivalent Perseverance data.
    2. Source: Curiosity waypoints and Perseverance waypoints.
    1. Shows the highest and lowest air temperature, plus air pressure, for the last 30 Curiosity REMS sols. A gap means the station did not report that value.
    2. Source: Curiosity REMS.
    1. Shows InSight’s last seven wind sols at Elysium Planitia: mean, lowest, and highest wind speed, direction, wind rose, and gust comparison. Outside Elysium, it is a reference rather than local wind data.
    2. Source: InSight weather
    1. Shows mapped dune fields with measured slip faces, including their identifier, number of measurements, and downwind direction. It represents the prevailing wind when the dunes were last substantially modified, not today’s wind.
    2. Source: Mars Global Digital Dune Database

Stack and Tools

We used as frameworks React Native and React for building the app. For the Mars Globe, we used the libraries Three.js and WebGL. For hosting, we used Vercel, and subscribed the domain in GoDaddy.

The app targets mobile and web.
